payload.name: Split-attention effect
payload.fact: The split-attention effect occurs when students must split their attention between multiple sources of information, which results in a heavy cognitive load.
payload.grade_basis: Corpus evidence = one primary study (Mousavi, Low & Sweller 1995), six experiments on geometry worked examples. Narrowed from the model's A: the clause 'increases extraneous working memory load' was not in any cited span, and the second citation (Ayres & Sweller 2005, The Split-Attention Principle in Multimedia Learning) was a design prescription -- 'it is important to avoid formats that require learners to split their attention' -- rather than evidence, so it was dropped from both provenance and source. Capped below the A band because a single-DOI basis is capped there unconditionally. The first provenance item is the paper's own premise, not its finding; the second item is the finding that the prediction built on that premise held across six experiments, which is why the record is graded on a confirmed premise rather than on an unchecked one. Grade reflects OUR corpus provenance, not the literature at large; to be re-graded when the computed rubric (D-114) lands.
